e.etymology: From Latin adorare, to adore or worship. It is related to Spanish Adoración, a name that honors the Adoration of the Magi.

assoc.t: Adora, the true identity of the cartoon hero She-Ra

e.etymology: An English surname from the medieval name Amis, Old French for friend, from Latin amicus. As a boy's name it follows surname names like Brooks and Hayes; Ames is also a nickname for Amy.

assoc.t: Ames, Iowa, home of Iowa State University
NASA's Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley

e.etymology: A spelling of Clay, an English surname for someone who worked with clay or lived on clay soil, from Old English claeg. Clay is also short for Clayton.
namesakes: Klay Thompson (NBA sharpshooter, four-time champion with Golden State)

e.etymology: From Arabic iman, faith or belief in God. The Emaan spelling is most common in Pakistani and other South Asian Muslim families.
A modern American coinage that adds the -lyn ending to Scott, a surname for a Scot or a Gaelic speaker. It arrived as Scottie caught on for girls.
A recent coinage of unclear source, close to Jeilyn and Jaylin. It has no established meaning.
A modern American name from the sound of the initials J.C., also used as a pet form of Jacqueline and as a feminine take on Jace.
From the English word for perfect happiness, Old English bliss. It was first a surname, from a nickname for a cheerful person, and is now a word name like Joy.

assoc.t: Bliss, the green-hill default wallpaper of Windows XP

e.etymology: A modern American name that reshapes Grace with the -yn ending of Kamryn and Jordyn. Grace is the English word, from Latin gratia, first taken up as a name by the Puritans.
Brought into use by the R&B singer Amerie, who broke out in 2002. It resembles Amery and Emery, medieval names of Germanic origin, but has no settled meaning of its own.
namesakes: Amerie (R&B singer of the 2005 hit 1 Thing)

e.etymology: From Latin mirabilis, wonderful or marvelous. It was given to both boys and girls in the Middle Ages, and Disney's Encanto (2021) brought it back through its heroine Mirabel Madrigal.

assoc.t: Mirabel Madrigal, heroine of Disney's Encanto

e.etymology: A recent American coinage that echoes Dior, the fashion-house name now given to babies, with an initial K. It has no established meaning.
From Irish Muadhnait, a diminutive of muadh, noble. In Scandinavia it is a short form of Monica or Ramona, and the Arabic name Muna, wishes, is often written Mona.

assoc.t: the Mona Lisa, Leonardo da Vinci's portrait

e.note: In Spanish mona means female monkey (and cute in some countries); in northern Italian slang it is a vulgar word.

e.meaning: fair-haired, or from the Isle of Bute
e.etymology: A Scottish surname, either from Gaelic buidhe, yellow or fair-haired, or from the Isle of Bute in the Firth of Clyde.
namesakes: Boyd Crowder (outlaw on the series Justified)
Boyd Holbrook (actor in Narcos and Logan)

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Susanna, from Hebrew Shoshannah, lily or rose, a word that goes back to the Egyptian name of the lotus.
The Roman goddess of wisdom, crafts and strategy, counterpart of the Greek Athena. Her name is traced to an Italic root for mind or understanding.
namesakes: Minerva McGonagall (Hogwarts professor in Harry Potter)

e.etymology: A modern American blend of Kai and the -lo ending of Kylo and Milo. An unrelated Kailo is an Estonian man's name.

assoc.t: sounds like Kylo Ren, the Star Wars villain

e.etymology: The French feminine of Yvon, a form of Yves, from a Germanic root for yew. Yew wood was used for bows, so the name may once have suggested an archer.
namesakes: Yvonne De Carlo (Lily Munster on The Munsters)
Yvonne Strahovski (actress in Chuck and The Handmaid's Tale)

e.meaning: a Wend, one of a Slavic people
e.etymology: A surname from a short form of Germanic names beginning with Wendel, a Wend, the Germanic word for their Slavic neighbors. In America it was often given in honor of the writer Oliver Wendell Holmes.
namesakes: Wendell Berry (Kentucky poet, novelist and essayist)

e.etymology: In Hebrew, Avia (Aviya) is the Biblical name Abijah, my father is Yahweh. American parents also use it as an elaboration of Ava, like Aviana.
A spelling of Odin, the chief god of Norse mythology, and the standard Swedish form of his name. Old Norse Odinn comes from a word for frenzy or inspiration.

assoc.t: sounds like Odin, chief god of Norse mythology

e.etymology: In American use a spelling of Bodhi, the Sanskrit and Pali word for the awakening of a Buddha. Bodi is also a Hungarian surname, from a short form of Boldizsar (Balthazar).
A spelling of Carly, a pet form of Carla and Caroline, feminine forms of Carl and Charles, from Germanic karl, free man. The -leigh ending follows Ashleigh and Kayleigh.
A modern name that pairs Ty or Tyler with the -la ending of Kayla and Layla. South African singer Tyla, who broke through with the song Water in 2023, lifted it in the United States.
namesakes: Tyla (Grammy-winning South African singer of Water)

e.etymology: A Mexican name, an elaboration of Nayeli with the opening sound of Ana. Nayeli is usually explained as Zapotec for I love you.
A Spanish-language name, a short form of Analía, itself a blend of Ana and Lía. Ana is the Spanish form of Hannah, Hebrew for grace.
e.note: The spelling begins with the letters anal, which can draw teasing in English-speaking schools.

e.etymology: A compressed spelling of Emery, an English surname and first name from the Norman Aimeri, from Germanic Haimric, home ruler, or Amalric, work ruler.
The Spanish-language spelling of Yvette, a French feminine diminutive of Yves, from a Germanic word for yew.
A pet form of Richard, from Germanic ric, ruler, and hard, strong or brave. Richie is also a surname taken from the same name.
namesakes: Richie Cunningham (Ron Howard's character on Happy Days)
Lionel Richie (singer of Hello and All Night Long)

assoc.t: Richie Rich, the comic-book boy billionaire

e.etymology: A modern American coinage in the family of Kamari, Jamari and Amari. It has no established meaning. Kemari is also the name of a traditional Japanese court ball game.
An older spelling of Dutch Hendrik and a Low German form of Henry, from Germanic heim, home, and ric, ruler. In English it is also a surname.
A modern American coinage that joins Kenz, from Kenzie and Mackenzie, to the -lee ending. It is close to Kinsley and Kensley.
